question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.

To renounce a throne
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Abdicate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Abdicate (verb) means to formally give up or renounce a throne, high office or responsibility. (त्याग करना / राजगद्दी छोड़ना)

◦ The one-word substitution asked for is exactly "to renounce a throne", which is the dictionary definition of abdicate.

◦ Correct: King Edward VIII chose to abdicate the British throne in 1936.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Avow means to declare or admit something openly and without shame. (खुलकर स्वीकार करना)

• Abort means to end or stop something before it is completed. (बीच में रोक देना)

• Assert means to state a fact or belief confidently and forcefully. (दृढ़तापूर्वक कहना)

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions: Coronation — the ceremony of crowning a sovereign; Abdication — the act of giving up the throne; Regicide — the killing of a king.

• Words often confused with abdicate: Abrogate (to repeal a law), Arrogate (to claim without right).

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

I have ______ to understand your problem.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. begun.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the present perfect tense, whose structure is have/has + V3 (past participle). (पूर्ण वर्तमान काल)

◦ The verb forms are: begin (V1) – began (V2) – begun (V3). After "have", only the third form begun can be used.

◦ Correct: I have begun to understand your problem.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "beginning" would need "have been" before it (present perfect continuous), which is absent here.

• Option 2 "began" is the simple past (V2) and can never follow "have".

• Option 3 "begin" is the base form (V1) and is used with "do/does/will/modal", not with "have".

NOTE

• Similar irregular V1–V2–V3 sets frequently asked in SSC: drink–drank–drunk, sing–sang–sung, ring–rang–rung, swim–swam–swum, shrink–shrank–shrunk.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

I am just saying that maybe you are letting emotion ______ your better judgment right now.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. cloud.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Cloud used as a verb means to make something unclear, confused or less able to function properly. (धुंधला कर देना / भ्रमित करना)

◦ Cloud one's judgment is a fixed collocation meaning to prevent someone from thinking clearly, which suits "letting emotion ______ your better judgment" perfectly.

◦ Correct: I am just saying that maybe you are letting emotion cloud your better judgment right now.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Clamp means to fasten or hold two things tightly together with a clamp. (कसकर जकड़ना)

• Clog means to block a pipe or passage so that nothing can pass through. (अवरुद्ध करना)

• Finger as a verb means to touch or feel something with the fingers. (उंगली से छूना)

NOTE

• Useful collocations with judgment: cloud/impair one's judgment, pass judgment, sit in judgment, against one's better judgment.

• Other idiomatic uses of "cloud": under a cloud (under suspicion), on cloud nine (extremely happy).

question:
Select the appropriate antonym for the underlined word.

Many children still do not have access to quality education that will harness their inherent abilities and talent.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. misapply.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Harness (verb) means to control and make productive use of something — especially a natural resource or an ability. (उपयोग में लाना / नियंत्रित कर काम में लेना)

• Misapply means to use something wrongly or for an unsuitable purpose, which is the exact opposite of using it properly. (गलत ढंग से प्रयोग करना)

◦ Correct: Education should harness, not misapply, a child's inherent abilities.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Direct means to guide or manage — close in sense to harness, so it is a synonym, not an antonym.

• Exploit means to make full use of a resource; it too is a near-synonym of harness in this context.

• Handle means to manage or deal with something, again a synonym rather than an opposite.

NOTE

• Synonyms of harness: utilise, channel, mobilise, employ, tap.

• Antonyms of harness: misuse, squander, waste, neglect, release.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where fruit trees are grown
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Orchard.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An orchard is a piece of enclosed land planted with fruit trees. (फलों का बगीचा)

◦ The phrase "a place where fruit trees are grown" is the standard definition of an orchard.

◦ Correct: Kashmir is famous for its apple orchards.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Dyke (dike) is a long wall or embankment built to prevent flooding from the sea or a river. (बांध)

• Botanical is an adjective relating to plants; the place where plants are grown for study is a botanical garden, so the bare adjective cannot be the answer.

• Cemetery is a burial ground for the dead. (कब्रिस्तान)

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions: Vineyard — where grapes are grown; Nursery — where young plants are raised; Apiary — where bees are kept; Aviary — where birds are kept; Granary — where grain is stored.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

The rise in temperature disturbs the rain cycle .
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. No improvement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is "The rise" (singular); the phrase "in temperature" is only a prepositional modifier and does not change the number of the subject. (कर्ता–क्रिया समन्वय)

◦ A singular subject in the simple present takes the -s/-es form of the verb, so "disturbs" is correct.

◦ Correct: The rise in temperature disturbs the rain cycle.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "was disturbed the rain order" mixes a passive verb with a direct object, which is ungrammatical, and "rain order" is meaningless.

• Option 2 "disturb the rainy cycle" uses a plural verb with a singular subject.

• Option 4 "disturbing the rain cycle" leaves the sentence without a finite main verb.

NOTE

• Rule: words between the subject and the verb (in/of/with/along with/as well as phrases) never affect the verb — "The quality of the mangoes was poor."

• "One of + plural noun" also takes a singular verb: "One of the boys is absent."

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

To fly into a rage
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To get very angry.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to fly into a rage" means to suddenly become extremely angry. (अचानक क्रोधित हो जाना)

◦ "Rage" itself means violent, uncontrollable anger, and "fly into" conveys the suddenness of the outburst.

◦ Correct: He flew into a rage when he saw the damaged car.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• "To harm oneself" is closer to the idiom to cut off one's nose to spite one's face.

• "To make inappropriate gestures" has no connection with rage and is a distractor.

• "To be very excited" describes happy anticipation, not anger — that is on tenterhooks / on cloud nine.

NOTE

• Anger idioms often asked in SSC: see red (become very angry), blow one's top / hit the roof (lose one's temper), make one's blood boil (infuriate), fly off the handle (lose self-control suddenly).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'no substitution required'.

Some of them were nearly (as hard as ligament, and many an inch in length).
option_1: as hard as ligaments, and many were an inch long
option_3: hard as ligament, and many an inch at length
option_4: as hard as a ligament, and many an inches in length
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. as hard as ligaments, and many were an inch long.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject is plural ("Some of them"), so the comparison must be with the plural countable noun "ligaments", and the second clause needs its own finite verb "were". (समानांतर संरचना)

◦ The comparison structure as + adjective + as is correctly completed as "as hard as ligaments".

◦ Correct: Some of them were nearly as hard as ligaments, and many were an inch long.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is wrong because the bracketed part is faulty — the countable noun "ligament" is used without an article and the second clause has no verb.

• Option 3 drops the first "as" (breaking the as…as structure) and uses the wrong preposition "at length".

• Option 4 says "many an inches", but many a/an is always followed by a singular noun.

NOTE

• Rule: many a + singular noun + singular verb — "Many a student has failed."

• Keep both halves of a compound sentence parallel and give each clause a finite verb.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

His ______ of smoking in restaurants created a lot of issues in New York.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. habit.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Habit means a settled or regular tendency to do something, especially one that is hard to give up. (आदत)

◦ The collocation "habit of + V-ing" fits the blank, and only a smoking habit would "create a lot of issues" in restaurants.

◦ Correct: His habit of smoking in restaurants created a lot of issues in New York.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Hatred means intense dislike; a hatred of smoking would not create problems in restaurants, so it contradicts the sense. (घृणा)

• Reputation means the general opinion held about someone; "reputation of smoking" is not idiomatic — one has a reputation for something. (प्रतिष्ठा)

• Orbit means the curved path of an object round a star or planet, and is contextually irrelevant. (कक्षा)

NOTE

• Habit collocations: in the habit of, kick/break a habit, out of habit, force of habit, creature of habit.

question:
Select the appropriate synonym for the underlined word.

There are actually many different versions of “Cinderella.”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Variations.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A version is a particular form of something that differs in some respect from other forms of the same thing. (रूपांतर / संस्करण)

• Variation means a change or slightly different form of something, which conveys the same idea. (भिन्नता / रूपभेद)

◦ Correct: There are actually many different variations of “Cinderella.”

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Problems means difficulties or matters needing a solution — unrelated to differing forms of a story. (समस्याएँ)

• Features means distinctive attributes or characteristics of something. (विशेषताएँ)

• Signals means gestures, actions or sounds that convey information. (संकेत)

NOTE

• Synonyms of version: rendering, adaptation, account, interpretation, variant.

• Do not confuse version (a form of something) with virgin, verse or aversion (a strong dislike).

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

The small amount of fusion fuel ______ to be heated to huge temperatures.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. needs.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The head of the subject is the singular noun "amount"; "of fusion fuel" is only a modifying phrase and does not decide the verb. (कर्ता–क्रिया समन्वय)

◦ A singular subject in the simple present takes the -s form of the verb, hence needs.

◦ Correct: The small amount of fusion fuel needs to be heated to huge temperatures.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "needing" is a participle and cannot act as the finite verb of the sentence on its own.

• Option 2 "need" is the plural/base form and does not agree with the singular subject "amount".

• Option 4 "needful" is an adjective meaning necessary, and an adjective cannot serve as the main verb here.

NOTE

• Quantity words followed by "of" take a singular verb when the head noun is singular: The amount/quantity/number of … is.

• But "A number of + plural noun" takes a plural verb: "A number of students are absent."

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

His struggles were becoming/ more and more frenzier,/ a wild look creeping into his blue eyes.
option_4: a wild look creeping into his blue eyes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. more and more frenzier,.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The adjective is frenzied (wildly excited or uncontrolled); its comparative is formed with more, not with the suffix -er, so "frenzier" is not a word. (उन्मत्त / अत्यंत उत्तेजित)

• A double comparative is also a grammatical error — you cannot use "more" together with an -er form. (दोहरी तुलनात्मक अवस्था)

◦ Correct: His struggles were becoming more and more frenzied, a wild look creeping into his blue eyes.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Segment 1 "His struggles were becoming" correctly uses a plural subject with the plural past continuous "were becoming".

• Segment 3 (option 4) is a correct absolute/participial phrase adding extra detail.

• Option 3 is wrong because the sentence does contain an error.

NOTE

• Rule: adjectives of two or more syllables usually take more/most; one-syllable adjectives take -er/-est. Never combine the two: ✘ more better, ✘ most easiest.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

I have to work in the morning, but I is freer in the afternoon.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. am free.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The pronoun I always takes the helping verb am in the simple present; "I is" is a basic subject–verb agreement error. (कर्ता–क्रिया समन्वय)

• After the linking verb "am", the positive-degree adjective "free" is used, since no explicit comparison with "than" is made in the sentence.

◦ Correct: I have to work in the morning, but I am free in the afternoon.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "is freed" repeats the wrong verb "is" and turns the clause into a passive meaning "set free", which changes the sense.

• Option 2 is wrong because the printed sentence does contain an error ("I is").

• Option 3 "am frees" wrongly adds a verb ending "-s" to what should be an adjective after "am".

NOTE

• Be verb agreement: I am, He/She/It is, We/You/They are (present); I/He/She/It was, We/You/They were (past).

• Use the comparative only when a comparison is expressed: "I am freer than my brother."

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.

Suspicion
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Conviction.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Suspicion means a feeling or belief that something is wrong, along with doubt or mistrust. (संदेह / शक)

• Conviction means a firmly held belief or complete certainty — the exact opposite of doubt. (दृढ़ विश्वास)

◦ Correct: He spoke with conviction, leaving no room for suspicion.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Niggle means a slight but persistent feeling of doubt or worry — a synonym of suspicion, not an antonym. (खटकने वाला संदेह)

• Tremor means a slight shaking or trembling movement, and is contextually unrelated. (कंपन)

• Incertitude means a state of uncertainty or doubt, again close in meaning to suspicion. (अनिश्चितता)

NOTE

• Synonyms of suspicion: mistrust, distrust, misgiving, scepticism, qualm.

• Conviction has a second meaning in law — a formal declaration of guilt by a court.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Losare.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Losare is not an English word; the intended spelling is Loser (one who loses) or Lose (to be deprived of / to be defeated). (हारने वाला)

◦ The other three options are all correctly spelt English words, so the misspelt one is Losare.

◦ Correct: He was a graceful loser who congratulated the winner.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Loss (noun) means the fact of losing something. (हानि)

• Local (adjective) means relating to a particular area or neighbourhood. (स्थानीय)

• Loose (adjective) means not tightly fixed or not fitting closely. (ढीला)

NOTE

• Commonly confused pair: Lose (verb, rhymes with "news") vs Loose (adjective, rhymes with "goose").

• Other frequently misspelt SSC words: occurrence, maintenance, committee, embarrass, privilege.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

To button one's lips
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To keep silence.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to button one's lips" means to stop talking or to keep quiet about something, as if the lips were fastened shut. (चुप रहना / मुँह बंद रखना)

◦ It is used chiefly as an instruction to say nothing, especially about a secret.

◦ Correct: The manager told the staff to button their lips until the deal was announced.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "To rain heavily" corresponds to the idiom to rain cats and dogs.

• "To advance in harmony" corresponds to to go hand in hand / to march in step.

• "To kidnap somebody" has no idiomatic link with lips and is a plain distractor.

NOTE

• Silence idioms: zip one's lip, keep mum, hold one's tongue, lips are sealed, maintain radio silence.

• Related: let the cat out of the bag and spill the beans mean the opposite — to reveal a secret.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.

Backstab
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Betray.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Backstab means to harm someone who trusts you, especially by treachery done behind their back. (पीठ पीछे धोखा देना)

• Betray means to be disloyal to a person or cause who has placed trust in you — the same idea. (विश्वासघात करना)

◦ Correct: A true friend will never betray you for personal gain.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Bleary is an adjective meaning (of eyes) dull or unfocused from tiredness. (धुंधली आँखों वाला)

• Berate means to scold or criticise someone angrily. (डाँटना)

• Blare means to make a loud, harsh sound, as a horn or loudspeaker does. (तेज़ कर्कश आवाज़ करना)

NOTE

• Synonyms of betray: double-cross, deceive, inform against, be unfaithful to, sell out.

• Antonyms of betray: protect, defend, safeguard, stand by, be loyal to.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.

Largest farmers usually have more money, social power and local influence.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Largest farmers usually.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence makes a general statement comparing two groups of farmers, so the comparative degree "Larger" (or the positive "Large") is required, not the superlative "Largest". (तुलनात्मक अवस्था)

• A superlative must be preceded by "the" and picks out one member from a whole group, which does not suit this general statement.

◦ Correct: Larger farmers usually have more money, social power and local influence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 3 "have more money, social power" is correct — the plural subject takes the plural verb "have".

• Option 4 "and local influence." correctly completes the list of three parallel nouns.

• Option 2 is wrong because the sentence does contain an error in its first segment.

NOTE

• Degree rules: comparative + than for two things; the + superlative + "of/in/among" for more than two.

• ✘ "He is the tallest of the two." ✔ "He is the taller of the two."

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: We can’t blame a bad goverment budget.
option_2: We can’t blame a bad governmnet budget.
option_3: We can’t blame a bad government budget.
option_4: We can’t blamme a bad government buget.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. We can’t blame a bad government budget.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Every word in option 3 is correctly spelt: blame, government and budget.

◦ Government is spelt with an n before the -ment ending (govern + ment), a letter very often dropped by candidates.

◦ Correct: We can’t blame a bad government budget.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 misspells "government" as goverment (the "n" is missing).

• Option 2 misspells it as governmnet (the letters "e" and "n" are transposed).

• Option 4 has two errors — blamme for "blame" and buget for "budget".

NOTE

• Remember the root: govern + ment = government; likewise environ + ment = environment (not "enviroment").

• Other frequently misspelt SSC words: parliament, questionnaire, entrepreneur, acquaintance, recommend.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.

I want all the culprits to be punished immediate.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. be punished immediate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Immediate" is an adjective and can qualify only a noun; here the word modifies the verb phrase "be punished", so the adverb "immediately" is required. (क्रिया-विशेषण)

• Rule: verbs are modified by adverbs, nouns by adjectives.

◦ Correct: I want all the culprits to be punished immediately.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 3 "I want all" is correct — "want" agrees with the subject "I".

• Option 1 "the culprits to" is correct; "want + object + to-infinitive" is a standard structure.

• Option 2 is wrong because the sentence does contain an error in its last segment.

NOTE

• Similar adjective/adverb pairs tested in SSC: quick–quickly, serious–seriously, careful–carefully, sudden–suddenly.

• Note the exceptions: hard/hardly, late/lately, near/nearly differ in meaning, not just in form.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

An 'occupational disease' is any disease (1)______ primarily by exposure at work (2)______ a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk (3)______ or to a combination of these factors. Occupational diseases are (4)______ those listed in national legislation as resulting from exposure to risk factors at (5)______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. caused.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank needs a past participle to form the reduced passive clause "any disease caused primarily by exposure at work". (कारण होना)

• Cause means to make something happen, and "caused by" is the fixed passive collocation used to state the origin of a disease.

◦ Correct: An 'occupational disease' is any disease caused primarily by exposure at work.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Abated means reduced or lessened in intensity, which contradicts the sense of a disease being produced. (कम होना)

• Posed means presented or created (a problem/threat) or adopted a position; "posed by exposure" does not fit the definition of a disease.

• Flawed means having a defect or imperfection, which cannot describe how a disease arises.

NOTE

• Passive collocations to remember: caused by, affected by, triggered by, brought about by, attributed to.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

An 'occupational disease' is any disease (1)______ primarily by exposure at work (2)______ a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk (3)______ or to a combination of these factors. Occupational diseases are (4)______ those listed in national legislation as resulting from exposure to risk factors at (5)______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The noun exposure takes the preposition to when naming the thing one is exposed to: *exposure to a risk factor*. (के संपर्क में आना)

• The sentence structure is "exposure at work to a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk factor", where "at work" tells the place and "to …" tells the agent.

◦ Correct: … caused primarily by exposure at work to a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk factor.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• "exposure in" would wrongly suggest a location rather than the agent of exposure.

• "exposure on" is not an accepted collocation in English.

• "exposure of" is used for the thing being exposed (exposure of the scandal), not for what one is exposed to.

NOTE

• Fixed prepositions with "to": exposed to, prone to, susceptible to, immune to, subject to, liable to.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

An 'occupational disease' is any disease (1)______ primarily by exposure at work (2)______ a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk (3)______ or to a combination of these factors. Occupational diseases are (4)______ those listed in national legislation as resulting from exposure to risk factors at (5)______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. factor.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Risk factor is a standard fixed compound in medicine and occupational health, meaning anything that increases the chance of developing a disease. (जोखिम कारक)

• The last line of the passage itself repeats the phrase "risk factors at work", which confirms that the blank must be factor.

◦ Correct: … exposure at work to a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk factor …

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• "risk exposure" reverses the word order and would repeat "exposure", already used earlier in the same sentence.

• "risk part" is not an English collocation and carries no meaning here.

• "risk maker" is not a standard term; the usual words are risk factor, risk taker or risk assessment.

NOTE

• Common "risk" collocations: at risk, run/take a risk, risk assessment, high-risk group, at one's own risk.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

An 'occupational disease' is any disease (1)______ primarily by exposure at work (2)______ a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk (3)______ or to a combination of these factors. Occupational diseases are (4)______ those listed in national legislation as resulting from exposure to risk factors at (5)______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. mostly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Mostly means for the most part or in most cases, and it correctly qualifies the general statement that occupational diseases are usually the ones listed in national legislation. (अधिकतर)

• The sentence needs an adverb of degree/frequency, not one of manner, because it describes how far the statement holds true.

◦ Correct: Occupational diseases are mostly those listed in national legislation …

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Radically means in a fundamental or extreme way, which does not fit a statement of general coverage. (आमूल रूप से)

• Oddly means strangely or unusually, giving a sense that contradicts a formal definition. (विचित्र रूप से)

• Manually means by hand, which is contextually irrelevant here. (हाथ से)

NOTE

• Similar adverbs of degree: largely, chiefly, primarily, generally, predominantly — all could replace "mostly" here.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

An 'occupational disease' is any disease (1)______ primarily by exposure at work (2)______ a physical, organisational, chemical or biological risk (3)______ or to a combination of these factors. Occupational diseases are (4)______ those listed in national legislation as resulting from exposure to risk factors at (5)______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. work.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage defines an occupational disease, i.e. one arising out of a person's job, so the risk factors must be encountered at work. (कार्यस्थल पर)

• The phrase "at work" is used earlier in the same passage ("exposure at work"), and repeating it keeps the definition consistent.

◦ Correct: … resulting from exposure to risk factors at work.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "at bank" is both ungrammatical (it needs "the") and irrelevant to occupational disease in general.

• "at office" is not idiomatic (correct form: "at the office") and it would wrongly limit the definition to office workers only.

• "at home" contradicts the whole idea of an occupational, i.e. work-related, disease.

NOTE

• Article-free place expressions: at work, at home, at school, in bed, in hospital, at sea — no article is used when the institution's purpose, not the building, is meant.
